turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr Hale. Come on through. It's the knee that's brought you, isn't it?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. The right one. It's been playing up.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Go on, then. How does it actually feel, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's a proper ache, deep in the knee. Worst going down the stairs. And it wakes me at night — I don't know, doctor, not every night, but a lot of them.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So pain in the right knee, worse on the way down the stairs, and often at night. Have I got that straight?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. Going up isn't so bad. Down is horrible. I'm seventy-one and I feel about ninety on those stairs.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did it start?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Not last week. Maybe since around Christmas? Or was it the autumn? I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right, we won't force a date. Any swelling you've noticed, or the knee giving way under you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling that I've seen. And it hasn't given way. It just hurts.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it lock, stick, and refuse to straighten?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any injury beforehand — a twist, a fall?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I didn't do anything to it. It just came on.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been putting on it, or taking for it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I rub in the Voltarol. The gel. Most evenings — well, actually not every evening, but most — and sometimes in the morning if it's bad.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diclofenac gel, on the right knee. And anything you swallow?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes those anti-inflammatory tablets from the chemist. Well, I say sometimes — maybe once or twice a week, I don't know, doctor. Just when I can't face the stairs.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse who booked you in has written diclofenac tablets, fifty milligrams. Is that what the box says?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty? I thought the packet was twenty-five. Or maybe it is fifty. I don't know, doctor. I just take one tablet when it's bad.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the nursing note says fifty milligrams, you remember twenty-five, and it's one tablet now and then. I won't guess which box you've got at home.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Sorry. I should have brought them.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble with them? Indigestion, a bleed, anything of that sort?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems at all.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And apart from the knee, how are you in yourself? Any fever, or the knee hot and red?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. It's not red. I'm just tired of it, that's all.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired of the pain, or a separate exhaustion, as if you're unwell?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): From the pain, I think. I don't know, doctor. I'm not ill.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it as you mean it. Do you take anything else regular?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, the odd two tablets, the five-hundred ones, if the gel isn't enough. And my water tablet in the morning, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet — do you know the name? Bendroflumethiazide, perhaps?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It's just the water tablet. Little white one. One each morning. Been on it for years.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, I'll record it as the water tablet until we see the box. You mentioned the blood pressure — that's still being treated?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, ongoing. The nurse checks it. I don't know the numbers.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Speaking of the nurse, she weighed you at ninety-one kilograms this morning.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-one? That can't be right. My bathroom scales said twelve stone four last Sunday. I don't know which to believe.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So ninety-one kilos on our scale, twelve stone four at home. I won't average them. Has the weight been creeping up, do you think?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe a bit. I don't know, doctor. I sit more these days, because of the knee.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): That fits with the knee. Before we go on — did you get here all right? The ring road was a nightmare when I came in.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, don't start me. I left at half eight and I was still crawling past the retail park at nine. Some lorry had shed a load of pallets.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pallets? On the dual carriageway?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Right across the inside lane. And the radio was on about the Test, and I nearly missed my turning because I was listening to the cricket.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who's playing? I haven't seen a ball all week.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): England, somewhere hot. My grandson was texting me the score every five minutes. He's mad for it. Twelve years old and he knows every bowler's average.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dangerous knowledge at twelve. Does he play?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Club cricket on Saturdays, when it isn't raining. Last week he was more interested in the tea than the batting, mind you.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tea is half the point. Anyway — back to this knee, if I may.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, sorry, I do go on.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Let me think out loud for a moment, and I am not making a firm diagnosis. This could be ordinary wear and tear in the joint, it could be a bit of cartilage grumbling, or it could simply be how the knee is loaded on the stairs. I am not going to conclude which of those it is, not today.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't know either?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not yet, and I'd rather say so. One thing from earlier — you said no stomach trouble. I just want to be sure about heartburn, acid, waking with a burn.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do get heartburn. At night, if I've eaten late. I didn't think of that as stomach trouble. It's been a few weeks, I suppose.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heartburn at night for a few weeks, especially after a late meal. That matters with those tablets. I'd rather you didn't take the diclofenac tablets for now.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): All right. The gel's fine, though?

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): The gel is reasonable to carry on with, on the knee, as you've been doing. And the paracetamol when you need it — up to two of the five-hundred milligram tablets, and not more than four times in a day.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I never take that many. Just the odd dose.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Now, two things we could do, and I am not choosing today. Physiotherapy, to work on the stairs and the strength. Or a steroid injection into the knee. Either might help. Neither is booked.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Needles aren't my favourite. But the stairs are awful.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we leave both on the table. If the pain is no better in six weeks, come back and we'll pick one. If it settles, you needn't rush back.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. And if it gets worse before that?
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it swells up hard, goes hot, or you can't walk, don't wait the six weeks — ring us sooner. That's the safety net.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I can do that.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back once more. Right knee pain, worse going down the stairs and at night, no clear start date. Voltarol gel most evenings. Diclofenac tablets now and then, and we still don't know if they're twenty-five or fifty milligrams. Heartburn at night. A water tablet each morning. The two weights don't agree. Physiotherapy or an injection, not decided. Come back in six weeks if it's no better.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): That's all of it. I think. I don't know if I forgot something.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you remember the tablet box, bring it next time. That's all I need from you.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll put it by the door so I don't forget.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Mind how you go on those stairs at home.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

omissions.text: Negative finding asked and answered: the knee was not hot/red; heat was specifically denied in addition to redness.
Negative finding: no indigestion/bleed or other stomach problems from the anti-inflammatory tablets was initially denied before heartburn was clarified later.
Plan/follow-up nuance: if the pain settles, the patient need not rush back.
